newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wages seen holding key to rate outlook.
newsitem.headline: Australian wages seen holding key to rate outlook.

text.p: Australia's interest rate outlook probably depends more heavily on wages growth than any other single factor at the moment, and markets will receive an update on that outlook with two key wages series due this week.

March quarter Department of Industrial Relations (DIR) data on enterprise bargaining agreements (EBAs) are due on Wednesday, and final average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) data for the three months to February will be released on Thursday.

Wages have been showing some signs of increasing recently, something about which Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Ian Macfarlane has expressed concern, given the low levels of inflation and high unemployment in the economy.

"These figures will need to be closely watched to assess the extent to which they represent a significant change in trend but, taken at face value, they suggest that wages growth has become uncomfortably high," the RBA said of recent wages data in its semi-annual monetary policy report earlier this month.

Given that, the general view amongst the markets at present is that official interest rates are going to be on hold at 6.00 percent for some time, possibly into 1998, despite the expected continued low inflation and high unemployment.
Macfarlane said last week the preliminary AWOTE data had been a setback to expectations of improving inflation.

That data showed a 1.3 percent quarterly rise, to be 4.6 percent higher over the year. With 4.5 percent annual growth seen as the Reserve Bank's 'line in the sand' on wages, the strong figure was enough for many to rule out a rate cut.

However, the final AWOTE data on Thursday will provide a breakdown of the pace of public and private sector wages. This split is important because private sector AWOTE, seen as a better indicator of inflation pressures flowing from wages, is running well below that of the public sector.
In the year to November, public sector AWOTE was 2.8 percent, compared to 7.6 percent in the public sector.
Public sector AWOTE has been artificially inflated by employment cutbacks of lower paid workers, producing a rate of wages growth above the rises paid in awards and EBAs.
Commonwealth Bank economists said their analysis suggested these changes had added at least two percentage points to public sector AWOTE since the middle of last year.
While there are doubts over AWOTE figures, there is a concern that the pace of EBAs has been rising recently.
The HSBC Markets wages report, released on Monday, forecast a rise in the pace of EBAs to around 4.65 percent in the March quarter, up from 4.4 percent in the December quarter.

HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said there was little evidence in the report to confirm a general acceleration, "but there is enough to throw serious doubt on the probability of a fourth rate cut."

Although the bearish words of the Reserve Bank on wages have lengthened the odds on another rate cut, analysts said signs of moderate wages growth may see increased speculation of a cut, especially the activity data shows signs of softness.

"If private sector wage growth is not as strong as previously thought, it leaves the door ajar for a rate cut if the economy remains stuck in third gear," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
Comments from Macfarlane last week that the RBA would let the economy run faster if it received good news on wages and inflation also gave the rate cut camp some hope.
"The bottom line is that wages outcomes will need to appear to be consistent with on-going inflation of around 2.5 percent for the RBA to act," Dredner chief economist Rob Henderson said.
"If this becomes clear over the coming week, then a rate cut should be factored in," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
